main.title: Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver
main.subtitle: Raziel moves between material and spectral worlds
main.summary: On August 16, 1999 Soul Reaver moved Legacy of Kain from a top-down perspective into a three-dimensional adventure centered on Raziel.

cards.heading: Betrayal sends Raziel across Nosgoth
cards.text: Released on August 16, 1999, Soul Reaver brought Legacy of Kain into a three-dimensional adventure centred on Raziel. Betrayed by Kain and transformed into a wraith, he travels across the gothic world of Nosgoth. Shifting between material and spectral states changes the shapes and routes available to him, making his condition central to exploration. Crystal Dynamics connects his pursuit of revenge with puzzles built around the two realms.

cards.heading: Puzzles between the material and spectral realms
cards.text: The player controls Raziel, a disfigured and ghostly vampire. The game is normally shown from a third-person perspective behind Raziel, but players can rotate the viewpoint around him. Gameplay relies largely on shifting between the material and spectral planes of existence to progress through areas. Although interaction with objects is limited in the spectral realm, this can be advantageous, because Raziel can phase through otherwise impassable gates there, and water is insubstantial, allowing him to walk on lakebeds; however, blocks, doors, and switches can be manipulated only in the physical realm. Many puzzles are based on the differences between the two realms; for example, platforms and environment features in one realm may change form to open new paths in the other. Block puzzles are also common and require the rotation, flipping, and moving of large blocks to progress, often with a time limit and while avoiding enemies.

cards.heading: Raziel gains new abilities
cards.text: At first, Raziel can jump, glide using his torn wings, move blocks, and pick up and throw objects and enemies. Initially unarmed, he fights using his claws, but can alternatively use weapons such as rocks, torches, spears and staffs, and the Soul Reaver. Raziel can freely shift to the spectral realm, but can return to the material realm only through special portals when at full health. Raziel automatically shifts to the spectral realm if he runs out of health. As the game progresses, Raziel gains the powers of his clan brothers after defeating them and becomes able to phase through gates in the spectral realm and climb walls in the material realm. Initially vulnerable to water, he overcomes this weakness and learns to swim.

cards.heading: Raziel, Kain and the Elder God
cards.text: The protagonist of Soul Reaver is the vampire-turned-wraith Raziel, whom Kain casts to death at the beginning of the game. Although Kain is the protagonist of the previous game, Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain, he is the primary antagonist and final boss of Soul Reaver. The Elder God resurrects and assists Raziel, explains the game's controls, and describes previous events in the story. Ariel, who preceded Kain as the guardian of the Pillar of Balance, appears as a spirit and offers Raziel advice on occasion. During his quest, Raziel meets his brothers - Melchiah, Zephon, Rahab and Dumah - who serve as the game's bosses. Each has developed different powers that Raziel partially gains by killing them and devouring their souls. A fifth brother, Turel, was omitted due to time constraints on development.

main.title: Re-Volt
main.subtitle: Small cars turn ordinary places into racetracks
main.summary: On August 18, 1999 Re-Volt arrived in North America and turned supermarkets, neighborhoods and domestic spaces into tracks for radio-controlled cars.

cards.heading: Radio-controlled cars at a different scale
cards.text: On August 18, 1999 Re-Volt arrived in North America and turned supermarkets, neighborhoods and domestic spaces into tracks for radio-controlled cars. Curbs, steps, shelves and ordinary objects become obstacles because the vehicle is small. Elastic handling, weapons and shortcuts create races that force players to read surfaces they would normally ignore. By changing the scale of the protagonist, Acclaim Studios London also changes the meaning of architecture and turns the everyday world into a collection of possible racing lines.

cards.heading: Radio-controlled racing in everyday places
cards.text: The premise of the game involves racing radio-controlled cars around environments like museums, steamships, construction sites and supermarkets. During a race the cars can collect random weapons to use to displace competitors. Cars and tracks were both unlocked through success in the game's tournament modes.

cards.heading: Championship cups and Time Trials
cards.text:
Championship - Racing in a cup which consists of four races for points. The higher the rank, the more points earned. However, the player is required to finish in 3rd or better to advance to the next race; failing to do so costs a try, and after three tries have depleted, the championship ends. Obtaining first in a cup unlocks additional levels and cars.

Time Trial - This game mode lets the player compete for the fastest lap time in any race that is unlocked. Beating the challenge time of tracks associated with a cup unlocks reverse, mirror and reverse mirror variations of those tracks.

cards.heading: The original PC car editor
cards.text: In October 1999, Acclaim Entertainment released the Re-Volt Car Editor which allowed players to export and edit, or create new cars for the PC version using 3D studio. The editor was simply discovered in the Acclaim Studios London office and as such was released as an unapproved and unsupported piece of code.

main.title: Dance Dance Revolution Solo Bass Mix
main.subtitle: Diagonal panels change the steps
main.summary: On August 19, 1999 Konami released Dance Dance Revolution Solo Bass Mix in Japanese arcades.

cards.heading: A single-player dance platform
cards.text: Konami released Dance Dance Revolution Solo Bass Mix in Japanese arcades on August 19, 1999. Two added diagonal panels support three- and six-panel layouts, changing where the player must step compared with the main series' four arrows. Much of its soundtrack comes from the Dancemania BASS albums, giving the single-player cabinet its own selection of music.

cards.heading: Three-panel and six-panel play
cards.text: Gameplay in the Solo series is nearly identical to that of the main Dance Dance Revolution series, but with a few differences to optimize the game for single-player mode.  In addition to the four-panel mode offered in the main series, Solo adds a three-panel mode in its Bass Mix and 2000 releases, as well as a six-panel mode in all of its releases.  Both modes add two new panels: up-left and up-right.  The three-panel mode adds the down arrow to these, while the six-panel mode combines both the four traditional panels and the two new panels.

cards.heading: Sixteen songs and the Dancemania BASS albums
cards.text: It was released as an arcade game by Konami on August 19, 1999 in Japan. The game premiered 16 songs to the series and takes its name, as well as most of its soundtrack, from the Dancemania BASS albums. This is the first game that features a live-action intro.

cards.heading: A separate Solo branch of Dance Dance Revolution
cards.text: Dance Dance Revolution Solo is a series of games spun off of the main Dance Dance Revolution series. It consists of three arcade releases in Japan. The game mode was also adapted for use in a children's arcade version and two console releases (as a game mode).

main.title: ISS Pro Evolution
main.subtitle: Football becomes a continuing club project
main.summary: ISS Pro Evolution is Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo's PlayStation football game, first released in Japan on 2 September 1999. It develops the series' on-field play while introducing club sides and the Master League. A match can now belong to a longer campaign in which a team is built and improved, giving the next fixture a context beyond an isolated victory. The clubs use city-based names rather than full official branding, but their role is clear. They turn the football game into something that can be returned to as an ongoing season and a personal project.

cards.heading: Football becomes a continuing club project
cards.text: ISS Pro Evolution is Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo's PlayStation football game, first released in Japan on 2 September 1999. It develops the series' on-field play while introducing club sides and the Master League. A match can now belong to a longer campaign in which a team is built and improved, giving the next fixture a context beyond an isolated victory. The clubs use city-based names rather than full official branding, but their role is clear. They turn the football game into something that can be returned to as an ongoing season and a personal project.

cards.heading: Make the next pass useful
cards.text: On the field, movement and passing create opportunities that a direct run towards goal may not provide. The player learns to recognise space, bring another teammate into the move and choose when to attempt the final ball. Club squads and international teams give different groups through which to practise those decisions. The largely unlicensed names and emblems mean presentation does not exactly reproduce the real competitions, but the relationships between players remain the centre of the experience. A good attack is assembled through several coordinated actions rather than one spectacular input.

cards.heading: The beginning of a familiar mode
cards.text: The original Master League includes sixteen club teams, making it a compact foundation for a feature that would become closely associated with Pro Evolution Soccer. Its progression gives results and team choices a continuing importance between matches. European and North American releases followed in 2000. The music is credited to a team including Akira Yamaoka and Shinji Enomoto. The game's significance lies partly in this shift of scale: football on the console becomes both the ninety-minute contest being played and the longer work of developing a team worth returning to.

main.title: Wild Arms 2
main.subtitle: A new team faces Filgaia’s crisis
main.summary: Wild Arms 2 first appeared on PlayStation in Japan on September 2, 1999, as Wild Arms 2nd Ignition. Ashley, Lilka and Brad introduce a new cast rather than continuing Rudy’s party from the first game. Their journeys lead into ARMS, a force confronting the organisation Odessa. Media.Vision brings this new cast into the series’ familiar frontier fantasy. Michiko Naruke returns to compose the music for this different journey through Filgaia.

cards.heading: A new team faces Filgaia’s crisis
cards.text: Wild Arms 2 first appeared on PlayStation in Japan on September 2, 1999, as Wild Arms 2nd Ignition. Ashley, Lilka and Brad introduce a new cast rather than continuing Rudy’s party from the first game. Their journeys lead into ARMS, a force confronting the organisation Odessa. Media.Vision brings this new cast into the series’ familiar frontier fantasy. Michiko Naruke returns to compose the music for this different journey through Filgaia.

cards.heading: Discovering places, choosing battles
cards.text: Exploration now includes a Search System for revealing towns, dungeons and hidden objects on the world map. Conversations and signs help narrow down where to look. Character-specific tools still solve puzzles, while a rotating camera can expose a passage hidden from another angle. Before some battles, a warning gives the player a chance to cancel the encounter; other warnings mean combat cannot be avoided. Turn-based fights also allow attacks against separate parts of certain bosses. The original two-disc adventure later reached digital services and PlayStation’s classics catalogue, preserving its own cast and systems.

main.title: Wipeout 3
main.subtitle: A future drawn with restraint
main.summary: Wipeout 3 is Psygnosis Leeds' PlayStation anti-gravity racing game, first released in Europe on 10 September 1999. Fast craft compete on futuristic circuits, using airbrakes, speed pads and weapons to manage both the route and the opposition. The Designers Republic helped give the game a restrained visual identity, extending a consistent language from menus to the racing world. Clean presentation supports an activity that quickly becomes demanding. The player must see the approaching turn, choose a line and make the craft follow it before the next wall arrives.

cards.heading: A future drawn with restraint
cards.text: Wipeout 3 is Psygnosis Leeds' PlayStation anti-gravity racing game, first released in Europe on 10 September 1999. Fast craft compete on futuristic circuits, using airbrakes, speed pads and weapons to manage both the route and the opposition. The Designers Republic helped give the game a restrained visual identity, extending a consistent language from menus to the racing world. Clean presentation supports an activity that quickly becomes demanding. The player must see the approaching turn, choose a line and make the craft follow it before the next wall arrives.

cards.heading: Keep speed without losing the line
cards.text: Steering an anti-gravity craft means allowing for its movement across the track rather than treating it like a car fixed to the road. Airbrakes tighten the approach to corners, while pickups add decisions about attack and defence. A small error can interrupt a promising lap, making practice on a familiar circuit valuable. Learning where to brake and where the course opens out gives speed a deliberate shape. The challenge comes from maintaining that rhythm while other craft and weapons introduce problems that cannot be solved by memorising the road alone.

cards.heading: Design and music share the same direction
cards.text: DJ Sasha selected an electronic soundtrack that includes Orbital and The Chemical Brothers, linking the racing atmosphere to contemporary club music. The game also supported widescreen and a high-resolution mode on the original PlayStation. Reviewers praised its graphics, music and minimalist presentation while noting its demanding difficulty. A European Special Edition in 2000 added further courses and content. As the last Wipeout on the first PlayStation, it brings that console's version of the series to a visually coherent conclusion before Wipeout Fusion moved to PlayStation 2.

main.title: Resident Evil 3: Nemesis
main.summary: Resident Evil 3: Nemesis is a 1999 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: Jill escapes Raccoon City
cards.text: Resident Evil 3: Nemesis is a 1999 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation. It takes place almost concurrently with the events of Resident Evil 2. The player controls the former elite agent Jill Valentine as she escapes from Raccoon City, which has been overrun by zombies. The game uses the same engine as its predecessors and features 3D models over pre-rendered backgrounds with fixed camera angles. Choices through the game affect how the story unfolds and which ending is achieved.

cards.heading: Nemesis pursues the player
cards.text: Resident Evil 3 was developed concurrently with Resident Evil – Code: Veronica (2000) and was conceived as a spin-off featuring a different protagonist. It was designed to have a more action-oriented gameplay than its predecessors and features a larger number of enemies. It also introduces Nemesis, a creature that periodically pursues the player.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Resident Evil 3 received acclaim and sold more than three million copies worldwide. Critics praised the setting, detailed graphics and Nemesis as an intimidating villain, but some criticized its short length and simple story. It was ported to Windows, Dreamcast, and GameCube with varying degrees of critical success. In particular, the GameCube version was criticized for its relatively high retail price and outdated graphics. A remake, Resident Evil 3, was released in 2020.

main.title: WinBack
main.subtitle: Omega Force · Nintendo 64
main.summary: WinBack is Omega Force's Nintendo 64 third-person shooter about Jean-Luc Cougar infiltrating a facility seized by terrorists. Their control of a laser satellite gives the mission a larger threat, but progress depends on surviving the immediate arrangement of corridors, guards and firing positions. Jean-Luc can take cover at corners and emerge to aim, making the environment part of his defence. The player repeatedly judges where it is safe to stand before committing to a shot that briefly exposes him to the opposing fire.

cards.heading: An operation fought from one safe position to another
cards.text: WinBack is Omega Force's Nintendo 64 third-person shooter about Jean-Luc Cougar infiltrating a facility seized by terrorists. Their control of a laser satellite gives the mission a larger threat, but progress depends on surviving the immediate arrangement of corridors, guards and firing positions. Jean-Luc can take cover at corners and emerge to aim, making the environment part of his defence. The player repeatedly judges where it is safe to stand before committing to a shot that briefly exposes him to the opposing fire.

cards.heading: Stop moving to line up the shot
cards.text: Aiming holds Jean-Luc in place while the stick directs a laser sight. Movement and firing therefore become distinct decisions, with a useful position established before the next target is engaged. Ammunition, weapons and opportunities to crouch or roll give the player additional responses to an ambush. Navigation also introduces keys and laser traps, making observation useful beyond combat. The next obstacle may ask for a shot at a control box rather than another enemy, connecting the same aiming system to progress through the facility.

cards.heading: A cover system before the later standard
cards.text: Released in 1999, WinBack gave console players an early example of building a third-person firefight around cover, exposure and a visible aiming line. Its PlayStation 2 adaptation followed in Japan in 2000, with revised presentation and multiplayer options. The original game later joined Nintendo's classic-game service. Its place in the genre's history comes from the clarity of that spatial relationship: an ordinary corner becomes a useful tactical object because it determines what the player can see, what can see them and when a shot can safely be attempted.

main.title: Age of Empires II
main.summary: Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings is a real-time strategy video game developed by Ensemble Studios and published by Microsoft.

cards.heading: Thirteen civilizations in the Middle Ages
cards.text: Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings is a real-time strategy video game developed by Ensemble Studios and published by Microsoft. Released in 1999 for Microsoft Windows and Macintosh in 2001, it is the second game in the Age of Empires series. The Age of Kings is set in the Middle Ages and contains 13 playable civilizations. Players aim to gather resources, which they use to build towns, create armies, and defeat their enemies. Five historically based campaigns present their own objectives and conditions. Three further single-player modes and multiplayer are also available.

cards.heading: An engine carried into a sequel
cards.text: Despite using the same game engine and code similar to its predecessor's, development of The Age of Kings took a year longer than expected, forcing Ensemble Studios to release Age of Empires: The Rise of Rome in 1998 instead. The design team focused on resolving significant issues in Age of Empires, but noted on release that some problems remained.

cards.heading: Acclaim and The Conquerors
cards.text: Reception of Age of Empires II was highly positive. The significant number of new features was praised, as were the gameplay improvements. Three months after its release, two million copies of Age of Empires II had been shipped, and it topped sales charts in seven countries. The game won multiple awards and is today considered a classic of its type, having had a significant impact on future games in its genre. The original Age of Empires II and its 2000 expansion pack, The Conquerors, were later released as The Gold Edition. Age of Empires II is often considered one of the greatest games ever made.

cards.heading: HD and Definitive editions
cards.text: An updated high-definition graphics version of the game, Age of Empires II: HD Edition, was released in 2013. The HD Edition includes the original game and the expansion The Conquerors, as well as new campaigns, civilizations, and updated graphics for high-resolution displays. A remaster, Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition, was released in November 2019.

main.title: Homeworld
main.subtitle: A Fleet Carries Its Home With It
main.summary: A real-time strategy game set in three-dimensional space, where ships and losses carry across a journey into exile.

cards.heading: A three-dimensional fleet campaign
cards.text: Homeworld brings real-time strategy into truly three-dimensional space, forcing players to think above and below the usual plane of the map. But its identity also grows from the continuity of the fleet: ships, losses and resources carry across missions and turn the campaign into a material journey. The mothership, the story of exile and a soundtrack designed to suggest distance and solemnity connect space warfare to the survival of an exiled people.

cards.heading: Commanding in three dimensions
cards.text: Ships can approach targets from above or below as well as from the sides. Commanding the fleet requires judging distance and formations across that volume. The interface lets players move between an overview and closer attention to individual groups, helping them plan an approach and understand how units are positioned around a target.

cards.heading: Protecting the mothership
cards.text: The mothership produces units and provides the fleet's continuing home. Protecting it is essential to the journey. Sending ships farther away may open opportunities but can also leave a threat closer to the centre of operations. Players have to balance those expeditions with the forces and travel time needed to defend the mothership.

cards.heading: Carrying the fleet into the next mission
cards.text: Ships, resources and losses carry from one campaign mission to the next. Preserving a vessel can strengthen the fleet for a later battle, while a costly victory can leave the next operation harder to manage. Decisions therefore affect both the current objective and the condition in which the fleet continues its journey.
